newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says tax reform to stimulate growth, jobs.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says tax reform to stimulate growth, jobs.

text.p: Germany's ruling coalition parties on Thursday gave their blessing to a big tax-cutting reform plan aimed at boosting the country's competitiveness and putting its four million unemployed back to work.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the reform would cut German taxes to the lowest level since World War Two and boost economic growth by half a percentage point per year.
"This is a decisive signal for investment and jobs," Waigel told a news conference called to unveil the reform.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl declared himself "very satisfied" with the reforms, which will take effect mainly in 1999.
Seeking to still critics among his own Christian Democrats (CDU) and the opposition, Kohl said they should first produce an alternative that would have "such a positive impact on small incomes."

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said the reform would raise German competitiveness. "Our tax reform concept is the most important answer to our economic problems: globalisation, weak investment, unemployment and over-regulation," he said.

After months of damaging wrangling, leaders of the three parties in Kohl's 14-year-old coalition approved a two-step plan to cut 82 billion marks ($50.04 billion) in taxes while scrapping an offsetting 38 billion marks worth of tax breaks.

The resulting tax cuts would be 44 billion marks -- more than the government can afford. Waigel wants to raise the 15 percent rate of value-added tax by one point to bring the net relief for taxpayers down to 30 billion marks.

But Kohl's CDU remains split on VAT, with a majority of its leadership wanting a two-point hike to help bail out the social security system. Regional party officials -- some facing elections -- are set against a VAT hike.
Christian Wulff, the CDU leader in Lower Saxony who has criticised plans for the VAT rise and even called for Waigel to resign, said he and Kohl had discussed their differences.
"I am by and large still opposed to an increase in VAT," Wulff told journalists. "I believe the dispute that I triggered was the right thing to do, especially in retrospect."
The CDU put off a VAT decision until February.

Opposition parties and lobbyists jammed journalists' fax machines with complaints that the changes would hurt low- and middle-income earners, pensioners and savers. Employer and industry groups, however, reacted more positively.

The package is "a mixture of reform, retouches and tricks," Joachim Poss, finance spokesman of the Social Democrats (SPD) told German Radio. The SPD has threatened to veto a VAT rise using its blocking majority in parliament's upper house.
The plan's main points look like this: Incomes below 13,000 marks for single earners would be tax-free from 1999. Pay up to 18,000 marks would be taxed at 15 percent.
Then, a sliding scale running from 22.5 percent kicks in, hitting a top rate of 39 percent at 90,000 marks.
The new income tax rates, to take effect in 1999, would cut existing rates running from 26 percent to 53 percent and bring the lion's share of the tax cuts.
The other big tax cut would be a two-step drop in corporate taxation. By 1999, retained profits would be taxed at 35 percent and profits paid out to shareholders at 25 percent.
That's the simple part. A coalition document listed over 70 revenue-sapping tax exemptions which are due to be cut.

The main items are: Reducing tax relief on Sunday, holiday and night work; tightening up on opportunity for companies to hide profits; cutting travel allowances; halving tax-free interest allowances and upping taxes on life insurance and pensions.

Although the coalition parties have agreed on the tax plan, it will have to go through several rounds of horse-trading in Germany's consensus-based political process. Finance Ministry officials said it may not even become law until next year.
